newsitem.title: USA: NY, NJ utilities seek relief from social taxes.
newsitem.headline: NY, NJ utilities seek relief from social taxes.

text.p: New York and New Jersey utilities, faced with open competition in their once-protected industry, are seeking ways to cut taxes levied against them that are used to fund social programs.

"We must work with legislatures to reduce that burden," Louis Peoples, chief executive officer of Orange and Rockland Utilities Inc, told a public symposium on electricity deregulation hosted by the utility.
Utility executives and regulators attending the symposium said New York state's electricity rates last year were about 40 percent above the national average.
These built-in costs are hampering their efforts to lower energy costs and improve their their ability to compete.
"Investor-owned utilities are not very good welfare agencies," said Peoples, explaining that the company's main responsibilities in a deregulated market are to shareholders, not the government.

Programs on energy conservation, renewable power, or assistance to low-income customers should be tossed back to the government or become market-driven, said utility executives and regulators taking part in a panel discussion.
They suggested that if these programs need to be funded by the energy industry, all energy paticipants - not just utilities - should contribute and help fund the programs.
"Funding of those programs should be maintained at current levels and reviewed every year," said Eugene Zeltmann, vice chairman of the New York Public Service Commission.
He estimated New York state's social policy programs receive several hundred million dollars in taxes tied to utility bills.

Neighboring New Jersey has already replaced a 13 percent gross receipt and franchise tax on utilities with a nine percent tax on net corporate income and a six percent general sales tax, said Herbert Tate, President of the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities.
He said the revised tax scheme would eventually cut the annual tax burden on the state's utilities by $500 million.

Tax relief may not come as quickly as the utilities would like. Both the New York and New Jersey state legislatures are currently grappling with other tax reduction plans which are likely to carve into needed public revenue.
"We're open to phasing it out," said Alex Gromack, a New York State assemblyman, referring to New York state's gross receipt tax on utilities.
But he noted that this kind of tax cut is competing in the Albany legislature with New York Governor George Pataki's proposed three-year $3.6 billion cut in the state's personal income tax.
-- R Leong, New York Power Desk +1 212 859 1622
